description: Databases fail loudly and specifically. Named exceptions, the EXCEPTION section, raising your own errors, and reading SQLCODE/SQLERRM — plus the one handling sin to never commit.

screens.body: In database programming, errors have NAMES. A failed lookup isn't 'something went wrong' — it's NO_DATA_FOUND. Too many rows? TOO_MANY_ROWS. These named conditions are called exceptions, and because they're named, your code can catch each one differently. Specific errors, specific responses.

options: A named error condition your code can catch
A syntax error in your SQL
check.question: An exception is…

screens.heading: Errors have names
screens.keyPoint: Exceptions are named error conditions — catch each one differently.

screens.body: Meet the usual suspects — predefined exceptions the database raises for you. NO_DATA_FOUND: your SELECT INTO found zero rows. TOO_MANY_ROWS: it found two or more (remember, INTO wants exactly one). ZERO_DIVIDE: math says no. DUP_VAL_ON_INDEX: you tried to insert a duplicate into a unique column. Learn these four and you'll recognize most real-world failures.

check.question: SELECT INTO returns 3 rows. Which exception fires?

code.snippet:
-- the usual suspects, predefined and ready to catch
-- NO_DATA_FOUND    : SELECT INTO found 0 rows
-- TOO_MANY_ROWS    : SELECT INTO found 2+ rows
-- ZERO_DIVIDE      : division by zero
-- DUP_VAL_ON_INDEX : duplicate in a unique column

screens.heading: Predefined: the usual suspects

screens.body: Catching happens in the EXCEPTION section at the bottom of your block. WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN ... handles that one error; WHEN OTHERS THEN ... catches everything else. Handlers run, and then the block ends gracefully instead of exploding. The error is still real — you're just choosing the response.

check.question: How do you catch a specific exception?

screens.heading: The EXCEPTION section
screens.keyPoint: WHEN <name> THEN … — pick your response per error.

screens.body: Sometimes the database's errors aren't specific enough for your business rules. Declare your own exception, then RAISE it when your rule is violated. It's just a name until you raise it — then it behaves like any other exception and can be caught by name in the EXCEPTION section.

options: It triggers the named exception immediately
It prints a warning and continues
check.question: RAISE my_error does what?

screens.heading: User-defined: invent your own errors
screens.keyPoint: DECLARE it, RAISE it, catch it by name.

screens.body: When your database logic is called by an app, the app needs to know WHAT went wrong. RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR lets you send back a custom error number (always between -20000 and -20999 — that's your reserved lane) plus a human message. Your Python or JS backend catches it like any database error, with your message attached.
screens.heading: RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR: talk to the app
screens.keyPoint: Custom errors: your number (-20000s) + your message, straight to the app.

screens.body: Inside a WHEN OTHERS handler, two built-in functions tell you exactly what happened: SQLCODE returns the error's number, SQLERRM returns its message. Log them, show them, include them in your own raised errors. An error you can name and quote is an error you can fix — 'something broke' helps nobody.

options: The name of the failed table
check.question: SQLCODE and SQLERRM give you…

screens.heading: SQLCODE & SQLERRM: the error's ID badge
screens.keyPoint: SQLCODE = the number, SQLERRM = the message. Log both.

screens.body: The classic sin: WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL. It catches every error and does NOTHING — silently swallowing failures. Data goes missing, balances go wrong, and nobody ever knows. If you catch, do something: log it, set a fallback, re-raise it. Handle, don't hide.

options: It only catches one error type
check.question: Why is WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL so bad?

screens.heading: Handle, don't hide
screens.keyPoint: Catching an error and doing nothing is worse than crashing.

screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: Oracle: PL/SQL 'Error Handling' · Postgres: 'Errors and Messages' + 'Trapping Errors' — same discipline, both dialects.

title: When the Database Says No
